objectives: Connect to neural language models + parsing.

slides.title: Syntax: structure of sentences
slides.body:
**Syntax** = rules + principles by which words combine into phrases + sentences. Native speakers reliably judge sentences as grammatical or not, generate novel ones, recognize ambiguity.

**Constituent structure**: sentences hierarchically organized into nested constituents (phrases). Tests for constituency:
- **Substitution**: 'the big red dog' → 'it' (pronoun substitutes for whole NP).
- **Movement**: 'I love the big red dog' → 'The big red dog, I love.' Constituents move together.
- **Coordination**: 'I love [the dog] and [the cat].'
- **Cleft**: 'It is [the dog] that I love.'

**Phrase types**:
- NP (noun phrase): the cat, my old computer.
- VP (verb phrase): runs, kicked the ball.
- PP (prepositional phrase): in the park.
- AP (adjective phrase): very tall.
- AdvP (adverb phrase): rather slowly.
- CP (complementizer phrase): that he left, whether to go.
- IP/TP (inflectional/tense phrase): the sentence with tense + agreement.

**X-bar theory** (Chomsky 1970, Jackendoff 1977): all phrases have same structure: [X' [specifier] [X (head)] [complement]]. NP head is N, VP head is V, etc.

**Phrase-structure rules** (older formalism):
  S → NP VP
  NP → (Det) (Adj) N (PP)
  VP → V (NP) (PP) (AdvP)
  PP → P NP

slides.title: Dependency vs constituency + word order
slides.body:
**Two main syntactic representations**:

• **Constituency / phrase-structure**: hierarchical tree of phrases. X-bar, GB, Minimalist, HPSG, LFG.

• **Dependency grammar**: directed edges between words (head → dependent). Simpler representation; flatter trees. Tesnière 1959; modernized in Universal Dependencies (UD, Nivre et al. 2014+).

Example sentence: 'The cat chased the mouse.'

Constituency tree:
[S [NP The cat] [VP chased [NP the mouse]]]

Dependency tree:
  chased → cat (subject)
  chased → mouse (object)
  cat → The (det)
  mouse → the (det)

Dependency representation is closer to predicate-argument structure; constituency closer to surface order + traditional grammar. Both useful for different analyses.

**Word-order universals** (Greenberg 1963):
- SVO (subject-verb-object): English, French, Mandarin, Russian. ~42% of languages.
- SOV: Japanese, Turkish, Korean, Hindi, Latin. ~45% of languages.
- VSO: Arabic, Welsh, Irish, Maori. ~9% of languages.
- VOS, OVS, OSV: < 1% each.

**Word-order correlations**:
- VO languages: prepositions; head-initial (head before complement); auxiliary-verb order; noun-relative order.
- OV languages: postpositions; head-final; aux + verb reversed; relative-noun order.

This is **Greenberg's universal 4** + related. Strong cross-linguistic patterns.

**Parameter setting** (GB / Principles + Parameters): innate grammar has parameters set by exposure. Head-direction parameter, pro-drop parameter, etc. Set by ~age 4 in children.

Modern Minimalist Program reduces parameters; emphasis on lexical + featural variation.

slides.title: Movement, displacement, + binding
slides.body:
Many languages allow elements to appear in non-canonical positions (movement / displacement):

• **Wh-movement**: 'Who did you see?' (object 'who' fronted).
• **Topicalization**: 'Beans, I love.'
• **Cleft**: 'It is John who left.'
• **Passive**: 'The cat was chased' (object becomes subject).
• **Raising**: 'John seems to be tall.'

**Bounding theory + islands**: extraction is restricted.
- Strong islands: complex NP, sentential subject, adjunct.
- Weak islands: wh-questions.
- Ross 1967 + Chomsky's Subjacency + extensions.

**Binding theory** (Chomsky 1981):
- **Anaphor (himself, herself)**: must have antecedent in same clause/local domain. ('John saw himself' OK; 'John knows Bill saw himself' = Bill, not John.)
- **Pronoun (he, she, it)**: free in local domain.
- **R-expression (John, the dog)**: free everywhere.

Reflects principle: closer dependencies preferred; longer-distance ones restricted.

**Coordination + parallelism**: 'I gave [a book to John] + [a pen to Mary].' Constituents must match in category + structure.

**Long-distance dependencies + neural models**: do LMs handle long-distance agreement, wh-extraction, NPIs?
- Linzen + Marvin 2016: LSTMs show some sensitivity.
- BERT + GPT: increasingly good at long-distance dependencies + multi-clause.
- Probing literature: hidden states encode syntactic structure (Hewitt + Manning 2019, structural probe).
- Edge probing, BLiMP (linguistic minimal pairs evaluation).
- Modern LLMs perform near-human on most grammaticality benchmarks but fail on some constructions (garden-path, NPIs in specific contexts).

Neural models + theoretical syntax intersect actively now.

question.question: Parse 'The cat that the dog chased ate the food' as constituency tree

steps.prompt: What's the main verb of the matrix clause?
hints: The action at the top level.
steps.reveal: **'ate'** is the main verb. Matrix clause structure: [The cat ... ate the food].
**'that the dog chased'** is a relative clause modifying 'the cat.' Structure: [NP [the cat] [CP [that] [IP the dog chased _]]].

steps.prompt: In the relative clause, what's the gap/trace position?
hints: What's missing in the relative clause?
steps.reveal: Relative clause has a gap (trace _) after 'chased': 'the dog chased _.' The wh-element ('that') is the displaced object; relativizes 'cat' as the chased one. Object-extracted relative clause.

acceptedAnswers: [S [NP [the cat] [RC [that] [S [the dog] [VP chased _]]]] [VP ate [NP the food]]]

steps.reveal:
Full constituency:
[S
  [NP [DET the] [N cat] [CP [C that] [IP [NP [DET the] [N dog]] [VP [V chased] [DP <trace>]]]]]
  [VP [V ate] [NP [DET the] [N food]]]
]

Or in dependency form: ate → cat (subject); ate → food (object); chased → dog (subject); chased → cat (relativized object); det → the; etc.

Object-extracted relatives are processing-difficult ('garden-path effect') vs subject-extracted ('The cat that chased the dog ate the food'). Subject relative often preferred + faster to parse.

question.question: Classify each language by its dominant word order.
question.explanation:
Word-order typology distribution (Dryer 2013, WALS):
• **SOV** ~45%: Japanese, Korean, Turkish, Hindi, Persian, Bengali, Tamil, Mongolian, Inuktitut. Geographically widespread.
• **SVO** ~42%: English, Mandarin, Spanish, French, Russian, Swahili, Indonesian. Found across all continents.
• **VSO** ~9%: Arabic (Classical), Welsh, Irish, Maori, Tongan, Hawaiian, Tagalog (partly). Concentrated in Polynesian + Celtic + Afro-Asiatic.
• **VOS** ~3%: Malagasy, Tzotzil (Mayan).
• **OVS** + **OSV** < 1%: very rare.

Flexibility varies: Russian + Latin highly flexible due to morphology; English rigid because no case marking. Modern Spanish + French SVO-dominant but allow inversion. Mandarin SVO but uses topic-comment structures heavily. Word order correlates with other typological features (head-direction, postpositions vs prepositions, etc., Greenberg + Hawkins universals).

question.question: Why does the sentence 'The horse raced past the barn fell' cause readers to 'garden-path' (mis-parse + then revise)?
options: Reader initially parses 'raced' as the main verb ('The horse raced past the barn'). When 'fell' arrives, parse fails — must reanalyze 'raced past the barn' as a reduced relative clause modifying 'horse' ('the horse [that was] raced past the barn'). Reflects local + greedy parsing strategy + processing limits. Famous example of syntactic ambiguity + reanalysis in psycholinguistics.
question.explanation:
**Garden-path sentences + parsing**:

*Example*: 'The horse raced past the barn fell.'

*Initial parse*: 'raced' as main verb past tense.
  → [S [NP The horse] [VP raced past the barn]]
  This is grammatically complete + fine. Reader expects period.

*Crisis*: 'fell' arrives. No way to add it to current parse. Reader stuck.

*Reanalysis*: 'raced past the barn' is a reduced relative clause modifying 'horse.' Full form: 'The horse [that was] raced past the barn.' Now 'fell' is the main verb.
  → [S [NP [DET The] [N horse] [VP raced past the barn]] [VP fell]]
  Now grammatical.

*Why this happens*:

1. **Greedy + local parsing**: human parser commits early to interpretation; doesn't backtrack until forced.
2. **Frequency bias**: 'raced' more frequent as past tense than as past participle in reduced relative.
3. **Reduced relative ambiguity**: 'raced' could be past tense or past participle; only context (verb following) resolves.
4. **Processing cost**: reanalysis is effortful + delayed.

*Other classic garden-paths*:
- 'The old man the boats.' (old man = noun phrase, then 'man' as verb).
- 'The complex houses married and single soldiers and their families.' ('complex' = noun, then 'houses' = verb).
- 'Fat people eat accumulates.' (people eat = sentence, but then accumulates needs subject... 'fat people eat' = noun-relative; subject is 'fat').
- 'The man whistling tunes pianos.' (whistling tunes = participle vs verb).

*Psycholinguistic models*:

- **Serial models**: parser commits to single analysis at each point. Garden-path arises when initial choice is wrong (Frazier + Rayner 1982).
- **Parallel models**: parser keeps multiple analyses ranked. Garden-path is when correct ranking is suppressed (Kim, Trueswell + others).
- **Constraint-based**: probabilistic integration of multiple cues. MacDonald + colleagues.

*Neural language models*:
- LSTMs + transformers show garden-path effects when probed.
- Surprisal at 'fell' is higher in models trained on natural text.
- Comparison to human reading-time data (e.g., Dundee corpus, GECO, MAZE). Neural surprisal correlates with reading time.

*Resolution mechanisms in humans*:
- Eye-tracking shows regression to 'raced' on garden-path sentences.
- Re-reading time on disambiguating region elevated.
- ERPs (event-related potentials): P600 component associated with syntactic reanalysis.

*Cross-linguistic*:
- All languages have garden-paths in various forms.
- Specific patterns differ by typology (head-initial vs head-final, reduced-relative availability).
- Bilingual processing: garden-paths may differ between L1 + L2.

*Implications*:
- **Writing pedagogy**: avoid garden-paths in clear writing.
- **NLP**: dependency parsing must handle ambiguity; PCFGs + transformer-based parsers.
- **Cognitive science**: garden-paths illuminate parsing mechanism + memory architecture.

Garden-path sentences are tiny windows into cognitive architecture; far more revealing than uniformly easy sentences.

hints: What's the initial vs final parse?
Why does the parser commit early?
slides.workedSolution: Garden-path: parser greedily commits to 'raced' as main verb past tense. When 'fell' arrives, must reanalyze 'raced past the barn' as reduced relative clause modifying 'horse'. Frequency bias toward past-tense reading; reduced-relative requires reanalysis. Resolution: eye-tracking shows regression; P600 ERP component. NLM: transformer surprisal correlates with human reading time. All languages have garden-paths; cross-linguistic patterns differ by typology. Mechanism illuminates greedy + local parsing + memory architecture.

question.question: Order these syntactic constructions by typical psycholinguistic processing difficulty (easiest to hardest).

items.label: Simple SVO declarative ('The dog ate the food.')
Subject-extracted relative ('The dog that chased the cat ran away.')
Object-extracted relative ('The dog that the cat chased ran away.')
Center-embedded relative ('The dog that the cat that the mouse saw chased ran away.')
Garden-path ('The horse raced past the barn fell.')

question.explanation:
Psycholinguistic processing-difficulty hierarchy (King + Just 1991, Gibson 1998, others):
• **Simple SVO declarative**: baseline; effortless processing.
• **Wh-question**: one displacement (wh-fronting); minor cost but transparent.
• **Subject-extracted relative**: relativized element is the relative-clause's subject; relatively easy (same-side dependency).
• **Object-extracted relative**: relativized element is relative-clause's object; harder due to longer dependency + crossing.
• **Center-embedded** (multiply nested): exponentially harder; ~3+ embeddings often un-parseable. Working-memory bottleneck.
• **Garden-path**: requires complete reanalysis; specific construction that misleads.

Factors driving difficulty:
- Memory load (Dependency Locality Theory; Gibson 1998).
- Frequency of construction.
- Predictability + surprisal at each word (Hale 2001).
- Working-memory capacity (individual differences).
- Bilingual + L2 effects.

Neural surprisal correlates with reading time + difficulty across these constructions. Modern psycholinguistics combines: experimental, computational (NLM-based), neuroscientific.

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain why understanding syntactic structure is foundational for modern NLP + LLMs.
question.rubric: Mentions: syntactic structure determines meaning ('Dog bites man' ≠ 'Man bites dog'). LLMs implicitly learn syntax via massive text exposure + transformer attention. Structural probes (Hewitt + Manning 2019) show hidden states encode dependency parses. BLiMP + other minimal-pair benchmarks: LLMs do well on agreement + binding + most syntactic phenomena. But some failures: garden-paths, NPIs in specific contexts, semantic-syntax interactions. Applications: machine translation requires understanding both languages' syntax; question-answering needs to identify subject/object/modifier; coreference resolution; semantic-role labeling. Constituency vs dependency: both formalisms support; UD (Universal Dependencies) provides multilingual treebank. NLP toolkits (spaCy, Stanford, Trankit) include parsers. LLM era: parsing as side-effect of language modeling; specialized parsers still helpful for structured tasks (info extraction, legal/medical NLP). Concludes: syntax + NLP increasingly co-evolved; both inform each other.
